doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Dressing like an entertainer and Leo's suit
summary: Ware recalls sharing a pressed suit and why musicians had to look the part.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: You can't, right. You go pick up the guys and ... I know bandleaders who tried to, you know, some cats they couldn't depend on, but they needed them because they could play. They would pick them up and do things like that just to make sure he would get to the gig on time. Even Leo. You know, Leo had a suit that I could wear it, as well as Nicky Hill Gilbert could. We didn't have a decent suit to look right on the bandstand, but Leo had his suit pressed, and I'd say there it is, and he made sure there were some holes in it so we couldn't pawn it. You know.

But that was important, even up until the sixties. In the sixties, people started to, well, I can't really say not caring how they looked -- but they started looking like the general society looked. It wasn't important to dress up anymore in the sixties when you saw them up on the bandstand. In informal attire, but earlier on, you did have to look a certain way.
Well, you had to look like an entertainer;
you would look like an entertainer, because it was a certain amount of flash, you know.
